questions.q: What gap does progressive delivery close, compared to the plain canary rollout from the previous lesson?
options: A plain canary paused at each step, but nothing automatically decided whether it was actually safe to advance based on real metrics
A plain canary cannot route any percentage of traffic to a new version at all
A plain canary always deploys to 100% of traffic immediately, with no steps
A plain canary requires manually editing the Kubernetes Service on every single deployment
questions.explain: The previous lesson's canary steps paused at each weight, but that pause was just a fixed timer — nothing checked real metrics to decide whether to advance or abort, which is exactly what progressive delivery adds.

questions.q: What does an Argo Rollouts `AnalysisTemplate` actually do?
options: It replaces the need for a Prometheus server entirely
It defines a metric query and a pass/fail threshold, run automatically at each canary step to decide whether to advance or abort
It only runs once, after the rollout has already reached 100%
It is a static YAML lint check that runs before the build stage
questions.explain: AnalysisTemplate defines a query (commonly against Prometheus) and a successCondition threshold, evaluated automatically at each canary step the Rollout references it from.

questions.q: In the error-rate AnalysisTemplate example, what does `successCondition: result[0] <= 0.01` mean?
options: The rollout waits 0.01 seconds between each check
The analysis fails unless exactly 1% of pods are canary pods
The analysis passes as long as the measured error rate (the query's result) stays at or below 1%
0.01 is the number of replicas required before analysis can run
questions.explain: The PromQL query computes the ratio of 5xx responses to total requests; successCondition says that ratio has to stay at or below 0.01 (1%) for the check to pass.

questions.q: What happens, according to this lesson, when the error-rate analysis breaches its threshold during a canary step?
options: Nothing — AnalysisTemplate only logs a warning and lets the rollout continue regardless
Argo Rollouts pages a human and waits indefinitely for manual approval before doing anything
The rollout immediately jumps to 100% weight to finish faster
Argo Rollouts aborts the rollout and shifts traffic back to the previous stable version automatically, without a human deciding first
questions.explain: That automatic abort-and-shift-back, with no human in the loop, is the entire point of wiring analysis into the rollout — catching a bad signal in minutes instead of waiting for someone to notice a dashboard.

questions.q: Besides error rate, what other kind of signal does this lesson say a realistic progressive-delivery setup commonly watches?
options: The total number of lines of code changed in the pull request
The number of GitHub stars on the repository
The color scheme of the internal admin dashboard
p95 or p99 latency, since a new version that's technically correct but noticeably slower is still a regression worth catching
questions.explain: Latency regressions can slip through an error-rate-only check — a version that returns correct responses but much more slowly is still a real problem, which is why latency percentiles are a common second signal.
